article.name: Create Context Graph

contact.note: The official pinned README was checked; it directs users to GitHub Issues and the Neo4j Community Forum and publishes no contact email.

article.contact_email_note: No contact email was published in the official pinned README.
article.summary: Create Context Graph is a Python CLI that scaffolds domain-specific agent applications with a graph memory layer. Generated applications can use hosted Neo4j Agent Memory Service or self-hosted Neo4j; this is a source review, not a runtime assessment.

who_what.text: The curated roster identifies ordinal 170 as Create Context Graph, slug create-context-graph, with an explicit repository locator; Atlas is retained only for roster attribution.

The official GitHub repository page showed main as the default branch and current head prefix 926e3b3; the official GitHub commit API resolved main to full SHA 926e3b3e7a2d3318f94e8a2cc5196677046bbe6d, with commit time 2026-10-09T14:51:25Z.
The official README describes an experimental scaffold generator maintained by Neo4j staff and community members; it is not a supported Neo4j product.
The pinned README was checked for email contact and lists GitHub Issues and the Neo4j Community Forum instead; no contact email is published there.

architecture.text: The ontology schema models domain metadata, POLE+O entity types and properties, relationships, document templates, decision-trace steps, agent tools with Cypher, and visualization configuration.
The generator renders a project scaffold from the selected ontology; the README describes a FastAPI backend, selectable agent framework, Next.js frontend, and optional MCP interface.
The README describes short-term message memory, long-term entity graphs, and reasoning memory made of decision traces; persistence differs between NAMS and Bolt backends.

behavior.text: Generated app message writes resolve a session identifier and call MemoryIntegration.store_message; the wrapper catches backend errors and returns no result on unavailable/unsupported paths.

NAMS fixture ingestion writes entity attributes into descriptions, serializes outbound relationship metadata in ccg-edges blocks, and records documents as both long-term entities and short-term messages. Bolt ingestion delegates to Cypher-based client operations.

Bolt mode exposes parameterized Cypher operations and a whole-database reset that DETACH DELETEs all nodes. The inspected message and REST adapter templates do not establish general per-record correction or deletion APIs.

The README describes context retrieval over messages, entities, preferences, and traces, as well as domain-specific agent Cypher tools and graph browsing. No recall quality or abstention evaluation was run.

The README documents reduced NAMS REST functionality, including the absence of arbitrary Cypher writes and native relationship writes; app client code uses domain predicates in selected graph operations, not all operations.

metrics.evidence: Context and graph retrieval paths are documented, but no answerable-recall workload was run.
No abstention behavior or workload was evaluated.
The inspected message wrapper and adapters do not define a general correction protocol; no correction workload was run.
A Bolt whole-database reset exists, but no post-deletion retrieval or storage-remnant check was run.
Domain filters appear in selected graph operations; there was no cross-project or tenant isolation workload.

limits.text: This review inspected selected scaffolder documentation, ontology/generation code, and shared memory/client templates, not every framework-specific agent, route, connector, or generated query.
NAMS behavior and isolation depend on a separate hosted service not audited here; generated code alone does not establish its access-control boundary.
Domain predicates in selected client operations do not establish comprehensive tenant isolation, particularly when arbitrary Cypher is available in Bolt mode.
The inspected files do not establish comprehensive per-record correction/deletion or physical erasure across backend persistence, derived artifacts, and backups.
No runtime, tests, benchmarks, or resource measurements were performed; source observations do not establish runtime retrieval quality or reliability.
